assertion: Zeus — Greek tradition makes Zeus ruler of Olympus and god of the sky, thunder and lightning.
Poseidon — Poseidon is the Greek god of the sea, earthquakes and horses, and his emblem is the trident.
Athena — Athena was the patron goddess of Athens, whose Parthenon honoured her on the Acropolis.
Artemis — Artemis is a virgin huntress in Greek religion and is commonly shown with a bow and deer.
Hephaestus — Hephaestus is the Greek god of fire, metalworking and craftsmanship, with a workshop imagined beneath volcanoes.
Heracles — Heracles completed the famous labours as service to King Eurystheus in Greek myth.
Achilles — Later tradition said Achilles was vulnerable at the heel, creating the expression “Achilles’ heel”.
Odysseus — Homer’s Odyssey follows Odysseus through many dangers on his voyage back to Ithaca.
Perseus — Athena’s reflective shield helped Perseus avoid Medusa’s petrifying direct gaze.
Theseus — Ariadne gave Theseus a thread so he could find his way out after confronting the Minotaur.
Medusa — Medusa is the mortal Gorgon whose severed head retained its petrifying power.
Pegasus — Pegasus is the divine winged horse associated with Bellerophon and the defeat of the Chimera.
the Minotaur — Greek myth describes the Minotaur as a human-bodied, bull-headed being confined in the labyrinth.
the Cyclops Polyphemus — Polyphemus is a Cyclops whom Odysseus blinds in order to escape from the cave.
Cerberus — Cerberus prevents the dead from leaving the underworld and the living from entering freely.
Jupiter — Jupiter was Rome’s chief sky and thunder god and was identified with Zeus.
Neptune — Roman Neptune was associated with fresh water and the sea and became equated with Greek Poseidon.
Venus — Venus was the Roman goddess of love and beauty; the planet carries her Latin name.
Mars — In Rome’s foundation myth, Mars fathered the twins Romulus and Remus with Rhea Silvia.
Mercury — Mercury was patron of merchants and travellers as well as the gods’ messenger, corresponding to Hermes.
Thor — In Norse tradition, Thor uses Mjölnir against giants and to protect gods and humans.
Baldr — Loki arranges for the blind god Höðr to throw the mistletoe weapon that kills Baldr.
Loki — Loki is an ambivalent trickster whose schemes solve some crises and cause others in Norse stories.
Freyja — Freyja belongs to the Vanir and is associated with love, fertility, battle and magical practice.
Týr — Týr placed his hand in Fenrir’s mouth as a pledge and paid the price when the binding held.
Fenrir — The gods fear Fenrir’s strength and use the magical fetter Gleipnir to restrain him.
Jörmungandr — Jörmungandr is so vast that it encircles the human world and grasps its own tail.
Sleipnir — Sleipnir is Odin’s exceptionally swift grey horse and a child of Loki in Norse myth.
the Valkyries — Valkyries serve Odin by choosing slain warriors, some of whom join the einherjar in Valhalla.
dwarfs — The dwarf brothers Brokkr and Eitri forge Mjölnir during a contest to create treasures for the gods.
Ra — Egyptian tradition imagined Ra crossing the daytime sky and journeying through the underworld at night.
Anubis — Anubis presides over mummification and helps conduct the judgement of the dead.
Osiris — The myth of Osiris’s death and restoration connected him with rebirth and the afterlife.
Isis — Isis is celebrated as a skilled magician, devoted wife and protective mother in Egyptian tradition.
Horus — Egyptian kings were identified with Horus, whose conflict with Set restored rightful rule.
King Arthur — Arthurian legend makes Arthur the ruler of Camelot and centre of the Round Table fellowship.
Excalibur — Excalibur is Arthur’s legendary sword, often given to him by the Lady of the Lake.
Merlin — Merlin developed from a figure in medieval Welsh tradition into Arthur’s magician and counsellor.
a selkie — Selkie tales often turn on a hidden seal skin that the transformed being needs in order to return to the sea.
a banshee — The banshee’s lament is traditionally heard as an omen that someone in a particular family will die.
amber — Amber from ancient tree resin has been collected and traded around the Baltic Sea for thousands of years.
the fern flower — Ferns do not truly flower, but folklore promises luck or hidden treasure to the person who finds the magical blossom.
a hiis — A hiis is a protected natural sacred place associated with communal rites and traditional belief.
Velnias — Velnias has roots in pre-Christian Baltic belief and later appears as a devil-like folklore character.
Jūratė — Perkūnas destroys Jūratė’s underwater palace after learning of her forbidden love, according to a familiar version of the legend.
Kalevipoeg — Kalevipoeg, the son of Kalev, is the central hero of the epic compiled by Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald.
Vanapagan — Vanapagan often appears as a strong but foolish opponent whom a clever human can trick.
a kratt — An Estonian kratt is animated through a pact with the devil and must be kept constantly at work.
näkk — The näkk belongs to a northern European family of water spirits whose beauty or music conceals danger.
Suur Tõll — Saaremaa legends make Suur Tõll a mighty protector whose landscape-shaping deeds explain local boulders and places.
Väinämöinen — Väinämöinen’s songs possess magical power, and his journeys frame much of the Kalevala.
the Sampo — The Sampo is a magical device that brings wealth to Pohjola until the heroes try to take it.
Louhi — Louhi is Pohjola’s formidable ruler, magician and principal opponent of the Kalevala heroes.
Ilmarinen — Ilmarinen is the master smith whose greatest achievement is forging the magical Sampo.
Kullervo — Kullervo’s cycle is one of the epic’s darkest stories, driven by abuse, revenge and disastrous recognition.
Genesis — Genesis contains the biblical creation narratives and begins the Jewish Torah and Christian Old Testament.
Chaos — Hesiod’s Theogony begins with Chaos, followed by powers including Gaia and Eros.
Ymir — The gods shape the ordered world from the primordial giant Ymir’s flesh, blood, bones and skull.
Brahma — Brahma is conventionally described as the creator, alongside Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer.
an egg — World-egg myths imagine the cosmos, a creator or the first beings emerging when a primeval egg opens.
Noah — Genesis says Noah builds the ark for his family and living creatures before the flood.
a rainbow — Genesis presents the rainbow in the clouds as the sign of the covenant after the flood.
the Epic of Gilgamesh — In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how he survived a divinely sent flood.
Zeus — In the Greek flood myth, Zeus sends the deluge and Deucalion and Pyrrha survive in a chest.
Vishnu — Matsya is Vishnu’s fish avatar, who guides Manu’s boat to safety during the deluge.
Anansi — Anansi comes from Akan tradition and became a central folk character across the African diaspora.
Coyote — Coyote can be creator, culture hero, fool or deceiver depending on the particular nation and story.
Raven — Raven is a transformer and trickster in many Northwest Coast traditions, including tales about bringing light.
Māui — Versions across Polynesia credit Māui with slowing or controlling the sun’s rapid journey.
a fox — Kitsune are magical foxes in Japanese folklore whose stories range from mischievous deception to loyal protection.
the Holy Grail — Grail romances turn the search for the mysterious vessel into a test of spiritual and knightly worth.
Jason — Jason commands the Argo and wins the Golden Fleece with crucial help from Medea.
Gilgamesh — Gilgamesh reaches Utnapishtim but learns that permanent human immortality is beyond his grasp.
Journey to the West — The pilgrims face monsters and trials on a legendary version of the historical journey to India.
El Dorado — The story began with a gilded ruler and grew into a legend of a fabulously rich lost city.
Pandora’s box — The earliest Greek text describes a jar; “Pandora’s box” became the familiar later expression.
Excalibur — In a familiar ending of Arthurian legend, a surviving knight casts Excalibur back into the lake.
Mjölnir — Mjölnir is Thor’s supernatural hammer, used against giants and carried as a protective symbol.
the philosopher’s stone — Alchemy credited the philosopher’s stone with transmutation and sometimes with producing an elixir of life.
Gungnir — Gungnir is Odin’s spear; its Old Norse name is commonly interpreted as “the swaying one”.
Saint George — The medieval legend of Saint George and the Dragon became a major image of heroic Christian knighthood.

assertion: Smaug — Smaug drives the dwarves from Erebor and guards their hoard until Bilbo’s company arrives.
Fafnir — Fafnir’s greed transforms him into a dragon, and Sigurd kills him from a pit beneath his path.
the Chinese dragon — Chinese dragons are generally auspicious beings connected with water, weather and authority.
Wales — The flag of Wales shows Y Ddraig Goch, the red dragon long associated with Welsh tradition.
Goliath — The biblical story contrasts the heavily armed Goliath with David’s sling and trust in God.
Paul Bunyan — Paul Bunyan is a gigantic lumberjack hero whose exaggerated adventures reshape the landscape.
jötnar — The jötnar are a diverse mythic group, not simply oversized monsters, and many gods have jötunn ancestry.
Fionn mac Cumhaill — A later popular legend explains the basalt columns as a causeway made by Fionn to meet a Scottish rival.
Stonehenge — Geoffrey of Monmouth linked Stonehenge to the Giant’s Dance in Ireland and said Merlin transported its stones.
Hades — In Greek tradition, Hades can mean the god and the underworld kingdom over which he rules.
Hel — Hel is both a female being and the realm assigned to her, distinct from the warriors’ Valhalla.
the Duat — The Duat is the Egyptian otherworld mapped in funerary texts as a place of nightly renewal and peril.
Xibalba — The Popol Vuh portrays Xibalba as a dangerous realm of trials ruled by death lords.
Japan — Yomi is the land of the dead in Japanese mythology, entered by Izanagi while seeking Izanami.
Mount Olympus — Greece’s tallest mountain became imagined as the divine seat of the Olympian gods.
Mount Sinai — Exodus places the covenant and giving of the commandments at Mount Sinai.
Mount Fuji — Fuji is sacred in Shinto and Buddhist traditions and has inspired pilgrimage routes and countless images.
Mount Kailash — Pilgrims perform a ritual circuit around Kailash, while climbing the mountain itself is discouraged.
Uluru — Uluru is a living cultural landscape whose features carry Aṉangu law, stories and ceremonial meaning.
Christianity — Christians understand Jesus as the Christ, and communities formed around his teachings in the first century.
Islam — Muslims regard Muhammad as God’s final messenger while also honouring earlier Abrahamic prophets.
Hinduism — Hinduism has no single founder and encompasses many philosophies, forms of worship and deities.
Buddhism — Buddhist traditions trace their teachings to Siddhartha Gautama, known after awakening as the Buddha.
Judaism — Judaism developed around the relationship between God and Israel expressed in the Hebrew Bible and later tradition.
Jesus — Christian teaching identifies Jesus of Nazareth as the Christ and Son of God.
the cross — The cross recalls Jesus’s crucifixion and, for Christians, the salvation associated with it.
baptism — Christian baptism uses immersion or pouring or sprinkling of water as a rite of initiation.
the Eucharist — Christian traditions celebrate the Eucharist in different ways while recalling Jesus’s meal with his disciples.
the Trinity — Trinitarian Christianity teaches that the three persons are distinct yet share one divine being.
the Torah — The Torah is Judaism’s foundational written teaching and is read publicly from a scroll.
rabbi — A rabbi is trained in Jewish law and tradition and may lead teaching, worship and community life.
Shabbat — Jewish Shabbat lasts from Friday evening until Saturday evening and is marked by rest, prayer and meals.
the menorah — The seven-branched Temple menorah is distinct from the nine-branched lamp used at Hanukkah.
kashrut — Kashrut is the system of Jewish dietary rules, while food permitted by those rules is described as kosher.
the Quran — Muslims regard the Quran as revelation from God delivered in Arabic to Muhammad.
Ramadan — Fasting during Ramadan is one of Islam’s Five Pillars, with exemptions recognised for particular circumstances.
Mecca — Mecca is Islam’s holiest city; Muslims face toward the Kaaba there during ritual prayer.
the hajj — The hajj takes place in a set month and includes rites at the Kaaba, Arafat and other sites.
zakat — Zakat is obligatory almsgiving intended to purify wealth and support specified groups in need.
karma — Karma literally concerns action and describes how deeds help shape future experience and rebirth.
dharma — In Hindu traditions, dharma varies with context but concerns conduct that upholds moral and cosmic order.
Brahman — Brahman is the supreme universal principle in major Hindu philosophical traditions and is not the same word as Brahma the creator deity.
samsara — Samsara is the continuing cycle of conditioned existence from which liberation is sought.
moksha — Moksha is spiritual release from samsara and is one of the major aims of human life in Hindu traditions.
the Buddha — Buddha is a title for one who has awakened; Siddhartha Gautama is the historical teacher at Buddhism’s origin.
the Four Noble Truths — The Four Noble Truths provide a basic framework for understanding the Buddhist path.
nirvana — Nirvana is the Buddhist goal in which the causes binding beings to suffering and rebirth are extinguished.
meditation — Buddhist meditation includes varied practices for calm, concentration, mindfulness and insight.
the Noble Eightfold Path — The Noble Eightfold Path is the practical fourth Noble Truth leading toward the end of suffering.
Guru Nanak — Guru Nanak taught devotion to one God, honest work, sharing and the equality of people.
Guru Granth Sahib — The Guru Granth Sahib contains hymns by Sikh Gurus and other devotional poets and holds final spiritual authority.
the Five Ks — The Five Ks are articles of faith worn by initiated Khalsa Sikhs as signs of commitment and identity.
the Khalsa — The Khalsa established a shared discipline and identity for initiated Sikhs under Guru Gobind Singh in 1699.
the Golden Temple — The Golden Temple is the common English name of the Harmandir Sahib, Sikhism’s foremost pilgrimage site.
Christmas — Christmas commemorates the Nativity of Jesus and is celebrated by most Christians in December or January.
Eid al-Fitr — Eid al-Fitr begins when Ramadan ends and is marked by prayer, charity, visits and festive meals.
Diwali — Diwali traditions vary by community but commonly feature lamps, family gatherings and celebration of light over darkness.
Hanukkah — Hanukkah recalls the rededication of the Jerusalem Temple; a new light is kindled on each night.
Vesak — Vesak is the major annual Buddhist observance of key events in Gautama Buddha’s life.
the Bible — The Christian Bible joins the books of the Old Testament with the specifically Christian New Testament.
the Quran — The Quran’s Arabic text is organised into 114 surahs of different lengths.
the Talmud — The Talmud combines the Mishnah with the Gemara’s extensive rabbinic analysis and debate.
the Vedas — The four Vedas are foundational śruti texts of Hindu tradition, with the Rigveda the oldest collection.
the Book of Mormon — The Book of Mormon is a foundational sacred text of the Latter Day Saint movement.
a church — A church building provides space for Christian public worship and community rites.
a mosque — A mosque is a place of Islamic prayer; congregational Friday prayer is a central weekly gathering.
a synagogue — Synagogues centre communal prayer and Torah reading and often provide space for study.
mandir — A mandir houses sacred images and provides a space for pūjā and other Hindu rites.
a meeting house — Quakers, formally the Religious Society of Friends, commonly call their places of worship meeting houses.
Socrates — Our knowledge of Socrates comes mainly through other writers, especially dialogues by his student Plato.
Plato — Plato’s Academy became one of the ancient world’s most influential centres of philosophical study.
Aristotle — Aristotle’s surviving works range across logic, ethics, politics, biology, poetics and metaphysics.
Confucius — Confucius’s teachings on humane conduct and social roles shaped East Asian thought for centuries.
Diogenes — Stories about Diogenes use provocative acts and radical self-sufficiency to express Cynic philosophy.
the Golden Rule — Versions of the Golden Rule appear in many religious and philosophical traditions as a standard of reciprocity.
altruism — Altruism contrasts with egoism by treating another’s good as a reason for action in itself.
utilitarianism — Utilitarianism treats the balance of benefits and harms for everyone affected as morally central.
deontology — Deontological theories hold that some actions are required or forbidden because of principles and duties.
virtue ethics — Virtue ethics focuses on cultivated character and human flourishing rather than a single rule or calculation.
a fallacy — A fallacy can sound persuasive while failing to provide the logical support its conclusion needs.
deduction — A valid deductive argument cannot have true premises and a false conclusion.
induction — Inductive support can make a conclusion likely without guaranteeing it, because a new case may differ.
a syllogism — A categorical syllogism links terms across a major premise, a minor premise and a conclusion.
Occam’s razor — Occam’s razor is a rule of parsimony: unnecessary entities or assumptions should not be multiplied.
King Midas — King Midas is remembered for the golden touch that made eating and drinking impossible.
Sisyphus — Sisyphus’s endless failed climb gave English the adjective “Sisyphean” for labor that can never be completed.
Cassandra — Cassandra could foresee disaster accurately, but the curse made her powerless to persuade others.
Tantalus — Tantalus’s unreachable food and drink are the mythic source of the verb “tantalize.”
Arachne — Arachne’s contest and transformation connect her name with spiders and their webs.
The Tortoise and the Hare — The Tortoise and the Hare rewards steady persistence after the faster hare wastes his lead.
The Boy Who Cried Wolf — The Boy Who Cried Wolf warns that habitual liars may not be believed even when they finally tell the truth.
The Goose that Laid the Golden Eggs — The Goose that Laid the Golden Eggs shows how impatient greed can destroy a continuing benefit.

assertion: The Fox and the Grapes — In The Fox and the Grapes, the failed attempt is rationalized by belittling the desired fruit, giving us the phrase “sour grapes.”
The Lion’s Share — The Lion’s Share supplies the phrase for the largest portion because the lion uses power to take the entire catch.
Saturn and Saturday — Saturday comes through the Roman tradition of Saturn’s day, making this the week’s clearest deity-name match.
Thor and Thursday — Thursday descends from Old English “Thunor’s day”; Thunor is the English form corresponding to Thor.
Odin and Wednesday — Woden is the English form of Odin, and Wednesday comes from Old English Wōdnesdæg.
Frigg and Friday — Friday comes from Old English Frīġedæġ and is traditionally associated with Frigg, although related goddess names complicate the etymology.
Týr and Tuesday — Tuesday derives from Old English Tīwesdæg, the day of Tiw, a Germanic form of Týr.
Starbucks and the siren — Starbucks describes its logo figure as a twin-tailed siren, also commonly called a mermaid.
Versace and Medusa — Versace’s logo centers on Medusa, a figure from Greek mythology.
Maserati and Neptune — Maserati’s trident was modeled on Neptune’s trident in Bologna’s Fountain of Neptune.
Goodyear and Mercury — Goodyear’s Wingfoot symbol was inspired by a Mercury statuette seen by founder F. A. Seiberling.
Mazda and Ahura Mazda — Mazda explains its name partly through Ahura Mazda, the Zoroastrian god associated with harmony, intelligence and wisdom.
Good Samaritan — A Good Samaritan is someone who helps a stranger in distress, after the charitable traveler in the parable.
forbidden fruit — “Forbidden fruit” refers both to Eden’s prohibited produce and figuratively to an attraction intensified by a ban.
prodigal son — The prodigal son is the returning younger child in Jesus’s parable and, figuratively, someone welcomed after an absence.
scapegoat — A scapegoat bears blame that properly belongs elsewhere, extending the ritual image of the sin-bearing goat.
writing on the wall — “The writing on the wall” is an unmistakable warning, from the message that foretold Belshazzar’s fall.
Ark of the Covenant — The Ark of the Covenant is the sacred chest linked in biblical tradition with the stone tablets of the commandments.
Shroud of Turin — The Shroud of Turin is a linen bearing a human image; its identification with Jesus’s burial cloth remains disputed rather than established fact.
Crown of Thorns — The Crown of Thorns belongs to the mockery of Jesus before the crucifixion and later became the subject of claimed relics.
Spear of Destiny — The Spear of Destiny, also called the Holy Lance or Spear of Longinus, is the legendary weapon associated with the wound in Jesus’s side.
Black Stone — The Black Stone, Hajar al-Aswad, is the venerated stone built into the Kaaba’s eastern corner.
Israel and the Star of David — Israel’s flag places a blue Star of David between two blue stripes on a white field.
Vatican City and the keys of Saint Peter — Vatican City’s flag displays the crossed keys of Saint Peter with the papal tiara.
Saudi Arabia and the shahada — Saudi Arabia’s flag shows the shahada in white Arabic script above a horizontal sword.
India and the Ashoka Chakra — India’s flag centers the 24-spoke Ashoka Chakra, a wheel derived from Ashokan symbolism.
Sri Lanka and the bo leaves — On Sri Lanka’s lion flag, the four bo leaves represent four Buddhist virtues: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity.
Holi — Holi is a Hindu spring festival widely recognized for exuberant play with colored powder and water.
Day of the Dead — The Day of the Dead, Día de Muertos, is a Mexican remembrance in which families honor deceased loved ones through offerings and festive imagery.
Ash Wednesday — Ash Wednesday marks the beginning of Lent in Western Christianity and is named for the ritual use of ashes.
Saint Lucy’s Day — Saint Lucy’s Day is especially associated with Swedish and Scandinavian candlelit processions led by a white-robed “Lucy.”
Obon — Obon is a Japanese Buddhist custom honoring ancestors, with lanterns used to welcome and guide spirits.
trolley problem — The trolley problem asks whether actively redirecting danger from five people toward one is morally permissible.
brain in a vat — A brain in a vat is imagined as receiving artificial inputs indistinguishable from ordinary experience, challenging what we can know about reality.
Pascal’s wager — Pascal’s wager argues pragmatically that the possible infinite gain from belief can outweigh its finite cost.
veil of ignorance — The veil of ignorance removes knowledge of one’s personal position so that principles are chosen without tailoring them to private advantage.
Russell’s teapot — Russell’s teapot illustrates that a claim does not become reasonable merely because others cannot disprove an undetectable object.
I think, therefore I am — “I think, therefore I am,” or “Cogito ergo sum,” expresses Descartes’s certainty that the thinking self exists.
God is dead — “God is dead” is Nietzsche’s famous diagnosis of the cultural consequences of declining Christian belief in modern Europe.

Hell is other people — “Hell is other people” appears in No Exit and reflects the play’s concern with being fixed and judged through other people’s gaze; it is not claimed here as the play’s final line.
The unexamined life is not worth living — “The unexamined life is not worth living” is the conventional rendering of Socrates’s statement in the Apology.

assertion: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains — “Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains” opens Book I by contrasting natural freedom with social constraint.
grandfather paradox — The grandfather paradox exposes a causal contradiction created when a journey into the past prevents that journey’s own cause.
liar paradox — The liar paradox arises because assigning either truth value to the sentence reverses that value.
omnipotence paradox — The omnipotence paradox tests whether unlimited power can consistently include the power to create a task that defeats itself.
barber paradox — The barber paradox is Russell’s accessible illustration of a self-referential rule that cannot consistently classify its own rule-follower.
sorites paradox — The sorites paradox shows how tiny individually harmless steps can make a precise cutoff impossible for a vague category.
Delilah — Delilah betrayed Samson after discovering that cutting his hair would leave him powerless.
Penelope — Penelope used the endlessly delayed weaving to keep her suitors waiting for Odysseus’s return.
Queen of Sheba — The Queen of Sheba is remembered for visiting Solomon and testing him with hard questions.
Esther — Esther used her position as queen to thwart Haman’s plot, a rescue commemorated at Purim.
Judith — Judith saved her city by beheading Holofernes after gaining access to his tent.
Book of Kells — The Book of Kells is an elaborately illustrated Gospel manuscript associated with Ireland and preserved at Trinity College Dublin.
Gospel of Judas — The Gospel of Judas is a Coptic Gnostic work that presents Judas very differently from the canonical Gospels.
Codex Gigas — Codex Gigas is exceptionally large and contains a striking full-page image of the devil, which inspired its nickname.
Diamond Sutra — The Diamond Sutra survives in a famous 868 printed copy discovered among the Dunhuang manuscripts in the Mogao Caves.
Codex Sinaiticus — Codex Sinaiticus is a fourth-century biblical manuscript closely associated with Saint Catherine’s Monastery in Sinai.
Pan and panic — Pan was believed to cause sudden, irrational terror, giving English the word panic.
Atlas and the atlas vertebra — The atlas vertebra supports the skull just as the mythic Atlas was imagined supporting the heavens.
Morpheus and morphine — Morphine was named for Morpheus, the Greek divine figure associated with dreams.
Rod of Asclepius — The Rod of Asclepius, a staff with a single serpent, is a traditional symbol of medicine.
Hygieia and hygiene — Hygieia was a goddess of health, and hygiene preserves her name in a modern health-related word.
Lourdes pilgrimage — Lourdes became a major pilgrimage centre after Bernadette reported visions at the grotto of Massabielle.

supportingSource.title: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes

assertion: Fátima pilgrimage — Fátima’s sanctuary grew from reports that three shepherd children saw apparitions of the Virgin Mary.
Kumbh Mela — Kumbh Mela is a major Hindu pilgrimage festival centred on bathing at sacred rivers and confluences.
St Olav's Way — St Olav’s Way is a network of pilgrim routes ending at Nidaros Cathedral, the traditional burial place of Saint Olav.
Bodh Gaya — Bodh Gaya is revered as the place where the Buddha attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi Tree.
Cassius Clay and Muhammad Ali — Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Clay and adopted his new name after joining Islam.
Saul of Tarsus and Paul the Apostle — The apostle was known as Saul and Paul; the sources use both names rather than describing a conversion-time renaming.
Cat Stevens and Yusuf Islam — Cat Stevens adopted the name Yusuf Islam after his conversion to Islam.
Malcolm Little and Malcolm X — Malcolm X was born Malcolm Little and used X to mark the African family name lost through slavery.
Lew Alcindor and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar — Kareem Abdul-Jabbar was born Lew Alcindor and adopted his Muslim name after converting to Islam.
Saint Nicholas and Santa Claus — Saint Nicholas was a bishop famed for secret gifts, and his tradition developed into Santa Claus.
Saint Patrick and the shamrock — Saint Patrick is traditionally associated with the shamrock as an illustration of the Christian Trinity.
Saint Christopher and travellers — Saint Christopher is traditionally regarded as the patron saint of travellers.
Saint Cecilia and music — Saint Cecilia is the patron saint of music and musicians and is often depicted with an organ.
Saint Anthony of Padua and lost things — Saint Anthony of Padua is traditionally invoked when lost things need to be found.
Noah and the dove — Noah sends out a dove, whose return with an olive leaf signals that the waters are receding.
Romulus, Remus and the she-wolf — Romulus and Remus are shown being suckled by a she-wolf in the Capitoline Wolf image.
Ganesha and the mouse — Ganesha is commonly depicted with a mouse or rat as his vehicle.
Saint Francis and the Wolf of Gubbio — Saint Francis is said to have made peace between the people of Gubbio and the Wolf of Gubbio.
Balaam and Balaam's donkey — Balaam’s donkey sees the angel first and speaks after Balaam strikes it.
Odysseus and the Sirens — Odysseus, also called Ulysses, survives the Sirens’ song by being bound to the mast while his crew use wax.
Job — Job endures devastating losses and illness in a biblical exploration of suffering and faith.
Lot's wife — Lot’s wife looks back at Sodom during the escape and becomes a pillar of salt.
Judgement of Paris — In the Judgement of Paris, Paris gives the golden apple to Aphrodite, a choice linked to the Trojan War.
Buddha and Mara — Buddha resists Mara’s temptations before attaining enlightenment.
gospel music — Gospel music developed strongly in African-American Christian worship and church life.
the Islamic call to prayer — The adhan is the Islamic call that announces the prescribed daily prayers.
Gregorian chant — Gregorian chant is the monophonic liturgical chant associated with the Roman Catholic tradition.
Hare Krishna mantra — The Hare Krishna mantra gained wide public recognition through ISKCON and a recording produced by George Harrison for Apple Records.
shofar — The shofar is a horn, traditionally made from a ram’s horn, used on major Jewish holy days.
Marcus Aurelius and Meditations — Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations gathers personal Stoic notes that were not originally written as a public book.
Viktor Frankl and Man's Search for Meaning — Viktor Frankl’s Man’s Search for Meaning combines his camp experiences with his ideas about finding meaning.
John Stuart Mill and On Liberty — John Stuart Mill presents his influential defence of liberty and the harm principle in On Liberty.
Simone de Beauvoir and The Second Sex — Simone de Beauvoir developed this influential analysis of women’s social condition in The Second Sex.
Hannah Arendt and Eichmann in Jerusalem — Hannah Arendt’s Eichmann in Jerusalem grew from her reporting on Adolf Eichmann’s trial and used the subtitle about the banality of evil.
Plato and platonic — Platonic love and friendship take their adjective from Plato, although the modern usage has developed beyond his own texts.
Freud and Freudian — A Freudian slip is named for Sigmund Freud and is interpreted in psychoanalytic theory as revealing unconscious material.
Machiavelli and Machiavellian — Machiavellian describes manipulative, calculating conduct and derives from Niccolò Machiavelli’s name.
Epicurus and epicurean — Epicurean derives from Epicurus, although his philosophy valued modest, durable pleasure rather than luxury alone.
Descartes and Cartesian — The Cartesian coordinate system is named for René Descartes, whose work linked algebra with geometry.
William Tell — William Tell’s famous ordeal combines his Swiss heroic status, his crossbow and the forced shot at the apple.
Pied Piper of Hamelin — The Pied Piper removes Hamelin’s rats, then returns to lead the children away.
Lady Godiva — Lady Godiva’s Coventry ride was intended to secure the remission of oppressive taxes.
Flying Dutchman — The Flying Dutchman is a ghost ship condemned to an endless voyage without making harbour.
Lorelei — Lorelei is the Rhine rock personified in literature as a singing woman who distracts boatmen.
Trojan horse — The Trojan horse hid Greek warriors inside its wooden body so they could enter Troy during the war.
crocodile tears — Crocodile tears name a show of false emotion linked to legends about crocodiles crying as they eat.
Sword of Damocles — The Sword of Damocles hung above the throne by a single hair while Damocles occupied Dionysius’s place.
Gordian knot — The Gordian knot was the challenge Alexander confronted at Gordium and famously cut apart.
Scylla and Charybdis — Scylla and Charybdis threaten opposite sides of the passage, so escaping one danger means approaching the other.
boogeyman — The boogeyman is used to frighten misbehaving children, and its description varies from one culture to another.
Sandman — The Sandman’s magical sand is placed in the eyes to bring sleep and dreams.
Easter Bunny — The Easter Bunny is a rabbit-like Easter visitor whose customary gift is eggs.
Tooth Fairy — The Tooth Fairy custom exchanges a lost tooth beneath the pillow for money or a small present.
Jack Frost — Jack Frost gives a human figure to frost, winter and cold weather.
Kraken — The Kraken is a Scandinavian legendary sea monster repeatedly associated with ships and sailors.
basilisk — The basilisk kills by looking at its victim, while mirrors and weasels appear in traditions about defeating it.
Baba Yaga — Baba Yaga belongs to Slavic folklore and inhabits the unmistakable chicken-legged hut.
Headless Horseman — The Headless Horseman is the mounted, headless figure made especially famous by Sleepy Hollow.
Krampus — Krampus comes from Alpine tradition and serves as the season’s punisher of naughty children.
four-leaf clover — The four-leaf clover is a rare mutation with four leaflets and is widely treated as a good-luck symbol.
crossing one's fingers — Crossing one’s fingers is a compact gesture used to wish for a favourable outcome.
knocking on wood — Knocking on wood is a superstition intended to prevent misfortune or preserve luck.
maneki-neko — Maneki-neko is a Japanese cat figurine whose raised paw is believed to beckon good fortune.
rabbit's foot — A rabbit’s foot is carried as a charm because it is believed in many places to bring luck.
Westminster Abbey — Westminster Abbey is the Westminster church traditionally used for British coronations.
Dome of the Rock — The Dome of the Rock stands in Jerusalem over the Foundation Stone and is marked by its gold-coloured dome.
Mont-Saint-Michel — Mont-Saint-Michel joins a Normandy tidal island with the abbey built on it.
Temple of Heaven — The Temple of Heaven is the Beijing ceremonial complex whose Hall of Prayer has a circular form.
Golden Pavilion — The Golden Pavilion belongs to a Kyoto Zen temple and has upper storeys covered with gold leaf.
Jesus Christ Superstar — Jesus Christ Superstar is the Webber-and-Rice collaboration written as a rock opera.
The Prince of Egypt — The Prince of Egypt tells the Exodus story in animation with Moses as its central figure.
Sister Act — Sister Act puts Goldberg’s character in a convent and centres its story on singing with the choir.
The Passion of the Christ — The Passion of the Christ presents Jesus’s Passion in Gibson’s film with extensive Aramaic and Latin dialogue.
The Ten Commandments — The Ten Commandments is DeMille’s Moses film and includes the crossing of the Red Sea.
Grim Reaper — The Grim Reaper gives death a hooded, skeletal form armed with a scythe.
Mother Nature — Mother Nature presents nature in maternal form and is also known as Mother Earth or the Earth Mother.
Lady Justice — Lady Justice represents justice through the scales, sword and blindfold associated with her.
Fortuna — Fortuna is the Roman goddess of luck and fortune; her wheel symbolizes life's changing fortunes.
Nemesis — Nemesis directs divine retribution at arrogance before the gods, and her name expresses giving what is due.
magic wand — A magic wand is the slender stick associated with performing magic in depictions of those figures.
crystal ball — A crystal ball is the spherical tool associated with fortune-telling and visionary scrying.
magic mirror — The magic mirror belongs to Snow White’s story and answers the queen’s question about who is fairest.
seven-league boots — Seven-league boots cross their namesake distance with every step.
cornucopia — The cornucopia is a horn-shaped emblem of abundance, traditionally filled with food and fruit.
Mother Teresa — Mother Teresa’s congregation and its blue-bordered white sari are closely identified with her work in Calcutta or Kolkata.
Pope Francis — Pope Francis is the Argentine Jesuit who chose the papal name Francis and was the first pontiff from the Americas.
Pope John Paul II — Pope John Paul II was Polish, travelled widely as pope and opposed communism.
Desmond Tutu — Desmond Tutu linked Anglican ministry and opposition to apartheid with leadership of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
Nick Vujicic — Nick Vujicic is an evangelist and motivational speaker born without arms or legs; his ministry is called Life Without Limbs.
horoscope — A horoscope applies the zodiac within astrology to offer a prediction or forecast.
fortune cookie — A fortune cookie encloses a paper message whose text can take the form of a prophecy or prediction.
palm reading — Palm reading examines the hand’s lines and treats them as signs of personality or what lies ahead.
dream interpretation — Dream interpretation reads symbolic meaning into dreams, which traditions have also used to predict events.
tea-leaf reading — Tea-leaf reading examines the shapes formed by leaves or dregs remaining in the cup.
unicorn — A unicorn is a legendary horse-like creature defined by a single horn on its forehead.
centaur — A centaur is a Greek mythological creature with a human upper body and a horse’s lower body and legs.
griffin — A griffin is a legendary lion-and-eagle hybrid; its name can also be spelled “gryphon”.
harpy — A harpy is a half-human, half-bird creature of Greek and Roman mythology that was often regarded as a personification of storm winds.
dryad — A dryad is a tree nymph or spirit from Greek mythology; the term originally referred especially to oak-tree spirits.
Friday the 13th — Friday the 13th occurs when a month’s thirteenth day falls on a Friday and is considered unlucky in Western superstition.
black cat — A black cat is a domestic cat with black fur whose superstitious meaning varies between bad luck and good luck.
broken mirror — Breaking a mirror is a familiar superstition said to bring seven years of bad luck.
walking under a ladder — Walking under a ladder is traditionally associated with bad luck, sometimes explained through the triangle formed by a leaning ladder.
opening an umbrella indoors — Opening an umbrella indoors is a common Western superstition; one proposed origin is the hazard of early metal-spoked umbrellas.
hijab — A hijab commonly means a head covering worn by some Muslim women, while the Arabic term also has a broader sense of modesty or separation.
turban — A turban is formed by winding cloth around the head and has many regional and religious forms, including an important role in Sikh faith.
kippah — A kippah is a brimless cap traditionally worn by Jewish men and boys and is also known as a yarmulke.
cassock — A cassock is a close-fitting Christian clerical coat or robe that reaches the ankles.
mitre — A mitre is tall, pointed ceremonial headwear worn by bishops and certain abbots.
sarcophagus — A sarcophagus is a coffin-like container usually carved in stone; the earliest stone examples were used by Egyptian pharaohs.
scarab — A scarab was a popular ancient Egyptian amulet shaped after the beetle and linked with the sun, regeneration or rebirth.
ankh — The ankh is an ancient Egyptian hieroglyph for life, shaped like a cross with a loop at the top.
Eye of Horus — The Eye of Horus is a stylized ancient Egyptian symbol associated with Horus and representing protection, health or restoration.
weighing of the heart — In the weighing of the heart, the deceased’s heart was weighed against Ma’at’s feather and the result determined the soul’s afterlife fate.
Jonah and the whale — Jonah is a biblical prophet who is swallowed by a large fish after being thrown overboard; popular culture often calls it a whale.
Tower of Babel — In the Tower of Babel story, people build a city and tower before their one language is confused into many.
burning bush — The burning bush appears in Exodus, burns without being consumed and is the place from which God speaks to Moses.
golden calf — The golden calf is the idol made by the Israelites while Moses is on Mount Sinai, an episode associated with idolatry.
Jacob's ladder — Jacob’s ladder is the Genesis dream of a stairway between earth and heaven on which angels ascend and descend.
ad hominem — An ad hominem attacks the person making a claim and avoids addressing the argument itself.
straw man — A straw man misrepresents an opponent’s argument so that the distorted version is easier to attack.
false dilemma — A false dilemma presents only two alternatives and ignores other available possibilities.
slippery slope — A slippery-slope argument links a first step to an insufficiently justified chain whose endpoint is often extreme or undesirable.
No true Scotsman — The No true Scotsman fallacy responds to a counterexample by redefining it as not truly belonging to the group.
free will — Free will is the capacity to choose actions, debated in relation to determinism and moral responsibility.
simulation hypothesis — The simulation hypothesis proposes that perceived reality is a computer-generated simulation and is discussed as skepticism about reality.
the problem of evil — The problem of evil asks how evil or suffering can coexist with an omnipotent and wholly good God and is central to philosophy of religion.
the mind–body problem — The mind–body problem concerns how mind, thought and consciousness relate to the body and physical world.
personal identity — Personal identity asks what makes someone the same person over time, with answers often involving bodily or psychological continuity.
yin and yang — Yin and yang are opposite yet interconnected forces in Chinese philosophy, represented by a circle of contrasting swirling halves.
crescent and star — The star and crescent combines a crescent shape with a star and became widely associated with Islam in modern times.
om — Om is a sacred sound and syllable important in Hinduism and other Indian religions, and its written form is widely used as a religious symbol.
hamsa — The hamsa is a palm-shaped protective amulet used in North Africa and the Middle East and also called the Hand of Fatima.
Dharma wheel — The Dharma wheel, or dharmachakra, is a widespread Buddhist symbol whose eight spokes represent the Noble Eightfold Path.
Bermuda Triangle — The Bermuda Triangle is a loosely defined North Atlantic region linked in popular stories to mysterious disappearances, although investigations find no unusual rate.
Fountain of Youth — The Fountain of Youth is a mythical spring whose waters are said to restore youth, one example of life-restoring water stories found in several traditions.
Area 51 — Area 51 is a secretive United States Air Force facility in Nevada that became central to UFO folklore and conspiracy theories.
Roswell — The Roswell incident began with debris recovered near Roswell in 1947 and later inspired claims of a crashed extraterrestrial spacecraft.
Shangri-La — Shangri-La is the remote Himalayan valley in James Hilton’s Lost Horizon whose name became a byword for an earthly paradise.
wedding veil — A wedding veil is worn by a bride over the head or face and belongs to wedding traditions in many cultures.
throwing rice — Throwing rice at newlyweds is a wedding send-off custom symbolizing prosperity and fertility.

something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue — The complete rhyme is “something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue”, and the named items are traditionally carried or worn by a bride.
breaking a glass — Breaking a glass traditionally ends a Jewish wedding ceremony: the groom crushes it underfoot and the guests respond with congratulations.
jumping the broom — Jumping the broom is a wedding tradition in which the couple jumps over a broom, strongly associated with Black and African-diaspora communities.
abracadabra — Abracadabra is a long-used incantation found in charms and amulets and strongly associated with stage magic.
sim sala bim — “Sim Sala Bim” was the three-word stage trademark of Dante the Magician, and its first and last words rhyme.
hocus-pocus — Hocus-pocus is a magician’s trick phrase and can also mean misleading nonsense or deception.
open sesame — “Open Sesame” is the magical phrase that opens the treasure cave in Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves.
Avada Kedavra — Avada Kedavra is the Killing Curse, one of the three Unforgivable Curses, and causes immediate death.
The Creation of Adam — Michelangelo painted this Sistine Chapel fresco, where God and Adam's fingers nearly meet.
Saturn Devouring His Son — Goya painted the work as part of his Black Paintings, depicting Saturn devouring a child.
Apollo and Daphne — Bernini’s sculpture depicts Apollo pursuing Daphne as she transforms into a laurel.
The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa — Bernini made the group for Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome, showing an angel visiting Teresa.
The Calling of Saint Matthew — Caravaggio’s painting hangs in the Contarelli Chapel and shows Christ calling Matthew from a tax collector’s table.
The Mummy — Stephen Sommers directed the 1999 adventure starring Fraser and Weisz, whose characters awaken the cursed priest Imhotep at Hamunaptra.
Troy — Brad Pitt plays Achilles in this adaptation of the Iliad and its ancient war story.
Clash of the Titans — The film follows Perseus, son of Zeus, on a quest that pits him against Medusa and the Kraken.
Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat — Andrew Lloyd Webber wrote the music and Tim Rice the lyrics for this musical based on the Genesis story.

assertion: Elektra — Richard Strauss composed the one-act opera to Hofmannsthal’s libretto, drawing its heroine from Greek myth.
Protestant Reformation — The Protestant Reformation began as a Western Christian movement and separated many Christians from Rome’s papal authority.
East–West Schism — The East–West Schism broke communion between the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches amid recurring Rome–Constantinople tensions.
Avignon Papacy — During the Avignon Papacy, popes resided in Avignon in the fourteenth century before the Western Schism.
St Bartholomew's Day massacre — The St Bartholomew’s Day massacre began in Paris in 1572, targeting Huguenots after the royal wedding.
Walk to Canossa — Henry IV travelled to Canossa in 1077 after Gregory VII excommunicated him, seeking absolution in winter.
Gregor Mendel — Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian friar whose pea experiments founded modern genetics.
Georges Lemaître — Georges Lemaître combined the Catholic priesthood with physics and proposed an expanding universe.
Joseph Priestley — Joseph Priestley was an English theologian who independently isolated oxygen in 1774 and investigated electricity.
Roger Bacon — Roger Bacon was a Franciscan friar who wrote on optics and stressed observation and experiment.
Thomas Bayes — Thomas Bayes was a Presbyterian minister and mathematician; Bayes’ theorem bears his name.
alien autopsy — Ray Santilli released purported alien-autopsy footage that aired on Fox in 1995 and was later thoroughly debunked.
The Blair Witch Project — The Blair Witch Project follows three students making a documentary, while its Sundance marketing listed the actors as missing or deceased.
Piltdown Man — Piltdown Man was presented as an early human from English remains until tests exposed the fraud in 1953.
Cottingley Fairies — The Cottingley Fairies appeared in five photographs made by two girls, who later admitted using cut-outs.
Donation of Constantine — The Donation of Constantine purported to grant papal authority, but Lorenzo Valla demonstrated that it was a forgery.
Sigmund Freud and Carl Jung — Freud and Jung exchanged 360 letters documenting early psychoanalysis before their relationship ended amid theoretical differences.
Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz — Newton and Leibniz developed calculus independently; Newton, then Royal Society president, wrote the committee report favouring his own claim.
Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr — Einstein and Bohr publicly debated whether the Copenhagen interpretation and complementarity adequately explained nature.
Noam Chomsky and Michel Foucault — Chomsky argued from innate structures and universal grammar, while Foucault stressed external and social structures.
Jean-Paul Sartre and Bertrand Russell — Bertrand Russell organised and Jean-Paul Sartre hosted the 1966 people’s tribunal on American policy and military intervention in Vietnam.
God of War — God of War is Santa Monica Studio’s action-adventure franchise about Kratos, shifting from Greek to Norse mythology.
Percy Jackson and the Olympians — The series adapts Rick Riordan’s novels about Percy, a demigod son of Poseidon who reaches Camp Half-Blood.

assertion: Assassin's Creed Odyssey — The game casts Kassandra or Alexios as a Greek mercenary descended from the Spartan king Leonidas.
Age of Mythology — Age of Mythology is an Ensemble Studios real-time strategy spin-off inspired by Greek, Egyptian and Norse mythology.
Black Myth: Wukong — Game Science developed the action RPG, which is inspired by Journey to the West and stars the monkey-like Destined One.
thorium — Thorium is element 90, named for Thor, and has been suggested as a uranium-replacement nuclear fuel.
cobalt — Cobalt is element 27; miners linked its ore name to a goblin, while the metal is used in blue compounds, alloys and batteries.
nickel — Nickel is element 28; its name recalls an ore that yielded no copper, and the metal is used chiefly in alloys and protective plating.
selenium — Selenium is element 34, named for Selene, and acts in humans as a trace nutrient and antioxidant-enzyme cofactor.
vanadium — Vanadium is element 23; Sefström named it for Vanadis, a name of Freyja, and small additions strengthen steel alloys.
Artemis I — Artemis I was the uncrewed 2022 lunar flight; NASA named the programme for the Greek Moon goddess and Apollo’s twin.
Juno — Juno entered Jupiter’s polar orbit in 2016, and its name recalls the goddess seeing through Jupiter’s clouds.
Chang'e 4 — Chang’e 4 and Yutu-2 made the first far-side lunar soft landing in 2019; the mission is named for a Chinese Moon goddess.
Phoenix Mars Lander — Phoenix landed in Mars’s northern polar region, confirmed water ice and reused hardware from a cancelled lander project.
Hera — Hera is ESA’s first planetary-defence spacecraft, sent to examine DART’s impact on Dimorphos and named for the Greek goddess.
Mahatma Gandhi — Mahatma Gandhi was imprisoned in South Africa and India, adopted satyagraha in Johannesburg and led India’s independence campaign.
Oscar Wilde — Oscar Wilde served two years after his gross-indecency conviction, wrote De Profundis in prison and later The Ballad of Reading Gaol.
Fyodor Dostoevsky — Fyodor Dostoevsky based the semi-autobiographical House of the Dead on convicts’ lives and his imprisonment in Omsk.
Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn — Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s Gulag sentence and exile informed work that exposed Soviet repression; he won the 1970 literature Nobel.
Viktor Frankl — Viktor Frankl founded logotherapy, survived Theresienstadt, Auschwitz and other camps, and based Man’s Search for Meaning on those experiences.
Dom Pérignon — Dom Pérignon is Moët & Chandon’s prestige cuvée, named for a Benedictine monk who improved wine but did not invent sparkling Champagne.
illuminated manuscript — An illuminated manuscript decorates text with borders and miniatures; strict illumination uses gold, and production moved from monasteries to urban workshops.
Trappist beer — Trappist beer is brewed in or under a monastery’s supervision; its authenticity label and non-profit rules support the monastery and charity.
Meteora — Meteora’s pillars hosted twenty-four monasteries, mainly founded from the later fourteenth century; six remain in the UNESCO-listed complex.
Mount Athos — Mount Athos is a northeastern Greek mountain and autonomous Orthodox monastic region whose traditions reach at least the ninth century.
March — March comes from Martius, which was named for Mars, the Roman god of war.
January — January takes its name from Janus, whose domains included beginnings and transitions.
September — September kept the name of its old seventh-place position even after it became the ninth month.
May — May is traditionally linked to Maia, identified with the fertility goddess Bona Dea.
February — February derives from Februarius and the purification rite called Februa.
ball lightning — Ball lightning reports describe long-lived luminous spheres associated with thunderstorms.
moonbow — A moonbow is a lunar-light rainbow; waterfall mist can supply the droplets that form it.
earthquake lights — Earthquake lights are reported around seismic activity, but their mechanism remains disputed.
will-o'-the-wisp — The will-o’-the-wisp belongs to bog-light folklore; proposed natural explanations include biological and chemical light.
St. Elmo's fire — St. Elmo’s fire is luminous plasma from a corona discharge and was treated by sailors as an omen.
infinity symbol — Wallis is credited with introducing the infinity symbol; he popularised it in a treatise published in 1655.
Pythagorean theorem — The Pythagorean theorem relates the squares on a right triangle’s sides and carries Pythagoras’s name.
Venn diagram — John Venn introduced the diagram that bears his name as a pedagogical tool.
Pascal's triangle — Pascal’s triangle arranges binomial coefficients and is named for Blaise Pascal.
Boolean algebra — George Boole developed Boolean algebra, whose two-valued logic underpins digital systems.
goodbye — Goodbye developed as a contraction of a blessing meaning “God be with you.”
adiós — Adiós joins a with Dios and is used for goodbye or farewell.
shalom — Shalom covers peace, welfare and safety and is used at both meeting and parting.
salaam — Salaam is the colloquial short form related to as-salamu alaykum.
Grüß Gott — Grüß Gott comes from a blessing wish in the Upper German-speaking region.
Like a Prayer — “Like a Prayer” features gospel vocals; its video includes a church and shows Madonna with stigmata-like wounds.
Losing My Religion — The title “Losing My Religion” is a Southern idiom, not a literal declaration about faith.
Take Me to Church — “Take Me to Church” pairs religious terminology with a story of a same-sex relationship facing violence.
Personal Jesus — Martin Gore connected “Personal Jesus” with Priscilla Presley’s memoir and personal devotion.
Jesus He Knows Me — “Jesus He Knows Me” is a Genesis song from We Can’t Dance (1991) and a satire of televangelism.
yoga — Yoga developed through diverse Indian traditions; exercise-focused forms centre on asanas and may include breathing.
sumo — Sumo wrestlers toss salt into the ring as symbolic cleansing, a ritual element linked to Shinto.
tai chi — Tai chi, or taiji, is practised in set sequences with gentle flowing motions; taiji also names the cosmological relationship of yin and yang.
capoeira — Capoeira has centuries of Black Brazilian practice and roots linked to Angolan engolo.
dragon boat racing — Duanwu is celebrated with dragon boat races; the best-known story in modern China says the festival commemorates Qu Yuan’s death.
Sorbonne — The institution takes its name from the Collège de Sorbon, created by Robert de Sorbon in 1253.

Salem witch trials — The Salem witch trials combined hearings and prosecutions across colonial Massachusetts.
Galileo affair — The Galileo affair concerns the Inquisition’s actions against Galileo’s defence of heliocentrism.
trial of Joan of Arc — The trial of Joan of Arc ended in execution; the later rehabilitation trial overturned its judgment.

Dreyfus affair — Zola’s open letter increased political support for Dreyfus and pressure to reopen the case.
Diana — Diana is both the goddess’s name and a feminine given name with centuries of use.
Michael — Michael derives from a Hebrew rhetorical question and appears as an archangel’s name in Daniel.
Theodore — Theodore comes from Theódoros and literally carries the sense “gift of God.”
Natalie — Natalie derives from natale domini; unlike Nathalie, the intended spelling has no h after the t and ends in -ie.
Dennis — Dennis and Denis derive from Dionysius, a name ultimately connected with Dionysus.
guru — In Indian traditions, a guru is a teacher or spiritual guide; in wider use, the word also means an expert.
taboo — Taboo can mark what a community treats as forbidden or set apart.
angel investor — An angel investor provides early capital, commonly for convertible debt or equity.
devil's advocate — The historical official challenged canonizations; the modern devil’s advocate tests an opposing case.
halo effect — The halo effect spreads one favourable impression across otherwise separate judgments.
Red Crescent — The Red Crescent became a formally recognised protective emblem in 1929.

assertion: meme — Dawkins introduced “meme” for a unit of cultural transmission that spreads through imitation.
agnosticism — Huxley coined “agnosticism” for the view that humans lack capacity for definitive knowledge about God and related matters.
identity crisis — Identity crisis belongs to Erikson’s account of adolescence; identity versus role confusion names the same response boundary here.
secularism — Holyoake used secularism for conducting life on naturalistic considerations without necessarily rejecting religion.
cognitive dissonance — Festinger proposed cognitive-dissonance theory and published A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance in 1957.
